claim: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for the most severe forms of human malaria.
source: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for the most severe forms of human malaria.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in malaria research, representing general scientific knowledge about P. falciparum pathogenicity.

claim: The intraerythrocytic asexual replication cycle of P. falciparum is approximately 48 hours.
source: Repeated rounds of its ~48 hr intraerythrocytic asexual replication cycle result in an exponential increase in parasite numbers and are responsible for all clinical symptoms of malaria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the P. falciparum life cycle timing.

claim: Repeated rounds of asexual replication result in exponential increase in parasite numbers.
source: Repeated rounds of its ~48 hr intraerythrocytic asexual replication cycle result in an exponential increase in parasite numbers and are responsible for all clinical symptoms of malaria.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of parasite multiplication dynamics.

claim: Asexual replication is responsible for all clinical symptoms of malaria.
source: Repeated rounds of its ~48 hr intraerythrocytic asexual replication cycle result in an exponential increase in parasite numbers and are responsible for all clinical symptoms of malaria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in malaria pathophysiology.

claim: At each round of replication, a small subset of parasites commits to differentiation into gametocytes.
source: At each round of replication, a small subset of parasites commits to differentiation into non-replicative sexual forms termed gametocytes, which are the only form transmissible to a mosquito vector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum sexual differentiation.

claim: Gametocytes are non-replicative sexual forms.
source: At each round of replication, a small subset of parasites commits to differentiation into non-replicative sexual forms termed gametocytes, which are the only form transmissible to a mosquito vector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gametocyte biology.

claim: Gametocytes are the only form transmissible to a mosquito vector.
source: At each round of replication, a small subset of parasites commits to differentiation into non-replicative sexual forms termed gametocytes, which are the only form transmissible to a mosquito vector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria transmission biology.

claim: Sexual commitment is marked by epigenetic activation of PfAP2-G expression.
source: Sexual commitment is marked by epigenetic activation of the expression of the master regulator PfAP2-G, a transcription factor of the ApiAP2 family (Josling et al., 2020; Kafsack et al., 2014; Llorà-Batlle et al., 2020; Poran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: PfAP2-G is a transcription factor of the ApiAP2 family.
source: Sexual commitment is marked by epigenetic activation of the expression of the master regulator PfAP2-G, a transcription factor of the ApiAP2 family (Josling et al., 2020; Kafsack et al., 2014; Llorà-Batlle et al., 2020; Poran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: PfAP2-G is the master regulator of sexual commitment.
source: Sexual commitment is marked by epigenetic activation of the expression of the master regulator PfAP2-G, a transcription factor of the ApiAP2 family (Josling et al., 2020; Kafsack et al., 2014; Llorà-Batlle et al., 2020; Poran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Sexual conversion is marked by the expression of gametocyte-specific proteins absent from any replicating blood stages.
source: This is followed by sexual conversion, which according to our recently proposed definitions (Bancells et al., 2019) is marked by the expression of gametocyte-specific proteins absent from any replicating blood stages.
evidence: This is based on definitions proposed in a cited publication by the authors.

claim: After sexual conversion, parasites develop through gametocyte stages I to V in a maturation process that lasts approximately 10 days.
source: After sexual conversion, parasites at the sexual ring stage develop through gametocyte stages I to V in a maturation process that lasts for ~10 days (Josling et al., 2018; Ngotho et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Immature gametocytes are sequestered in organs such as the bone marrow.
source: While immature gametocytes are sequestered in organs such as the bone marrow (Venugopal et al., 2020), mature gametocytes (stage V) are released into the circulation, where they are infectious to mosquitoes for several days or even weeks (Cao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mature gametocytes (stage V) are released into the circulation.
source: While immature gametocytes are sequestered in organs such as the bone marrow (Venugopal et al., 2020), mature gametocytes (stage V) are released into the circulation, where they are infectious to mosquitoes for several days or even weeks (Cao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mature gametocytes are infectious to mosquitoes for several days or even weeks.
source: While immature gametocytes are sequestered in organs such as the bone marrow (Venugopal et al., 2020), mature gametocytes (stage V) are released into the circulation, where they are infectious to mosquitoes for several days or even weeks (Cao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The World Health Organization has adopted malaria elimination as a global goal.
source: To eliminate malaria, which the World Health Organization has adopted as a global goal, it is necessary to block transmission, as well as killing asexual parasites to cure patients (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a WHO document.

claim: To eliminate malaria, it is necessary to block transmission and kill asexual parasites to cure patients.
source: To eliminate malaria, which the World Health Organization has adopted as a global goal, it is necessary to block transmission, as well as killing asexual parasites to cure patients (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a WHO document and represents established understanding of malaria control strategies.

claim: The sexual conversion rate is the proportion of parasites that convert into sexual forms at each replicative cycle.
source: To secure within-host survival and between-host transmission, the proportion of parasites that convert into sexual forms at each replicative cycle, termed sexual conversion rate, is variable and tightly regulated.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: The sexual conversion rate is variable and tightly regulated.
source: To secure within-host survival and between-host transmission, the proportion of parasites that convert into sexual forms at each replicative cycle, termed sexual conversion rate, is variable and tightly regulated.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of parasite biology.

claim: In human infections, gametocyte densities are always much lower than asexual parasite densities.
source: In human infections, gametocyte densities are always much lower than asexual parasite densities, and basal P. falciparum sexual conversion rates in vivo are estimated to be ~1% (Cao et al., 2019; Eichner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Basal P. falciparum sexual conversion rates in vivo are estimated to be approximately 1%.
source: In human infections, gametocyte densities are always much lower than asexual parasite densities, and basal P. falciparum sexual conversion rates in vivo are estimated to be ~1% (Cao et al., 2019; Eichner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Low sexual conversion rates reveal a reproductive restraint for which multiple alternative hypotheses have been proposed.
source: This reveals a reproductive restraint for which multiple alternative hypotheses have been proposed (McKenzie and Bossert, 1998; Mideo and Day, 2008; Taylor and Read, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Multiple observations suggest that malaria parasites can respond to changes in environmental conditions by adjusting the trade-off between transmission and within-host survival.
source: Whatever the reason for the low levels of sexual conversion, multiple observations suggest that malaria parasites can respond to changes in the conditions of their environment by adjusting the trade-off between transmission and within-host survival.
evidence: This is based on inference from multiple observations in the field.

claim: The ability to adjust sexual conversion rates depending on host conditions would be clearly advantageous for the parasite from an evolutionary perspective.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, the ability to adjust sexual conversion rates depending on the host conditions would be clearly advantageous for the parasite (Carter et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and represents evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Several conditions have been shown to increase sexual conversion rates in P. falciparum.
source: In P. falciparum, several conditions have been shown to increase sexual conversion rates, and sexual conversion is viewed by some as a response to stress, although this remains controversial (Baker, 2010; Bousema and Drakeley, 2011; Dyer and Day, 2000; Josling et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sexual conversion is viewed by some as a response to stress, although this remains controversial.
source: In P. falciparum, several conditions have been shown to increase sexual conversion rates, and sexual conversion is viewed by some as a response to stress, although this remains controversial (Baker, 2010; Bousema and Drakeley, 2011; Dyer and Day, 2000; Josling et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and acknowledges ongoing debate.

claim: The most commonly used method to enhance sexual conversion in vitro relies on overgrowing blood-stage cultures (the 'crash method').
source: The most commonly used method to enhance sexual conversion and obtain large numbers of gametocytes in vitro relies on overgrowing blood-stage cultures (the 'crash method') (Delves et al., 2016) and/or maintaining the cultures with parasite-conditioned (spent) medium (Brancucci et al., 2015; Fivelman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Depletion of lysophosphatidylcholine (LysoPC) underlies the stimulation of sexual conversion by high asexual parasitemia or spent medium.
source: Recent research has established that depletion of the human serum lipid lysophosphatidylcholine (LysoPC) underlies the stimulation of sexual conversion by high asexual parasitemia or spent medium, providing the first mechanistic insight into how environmental conditions can influence the rate of sexual conversion (Brancucci et al., 2018; Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Low plasma LysoPC levels were associated with increased sexual conversion rates in human infections.
source: Low plasma LysoPC levels were also associated with increased sexual conversion rates in human infections (Usui et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Depletion of LysoPC or choline has been used by several groups to stimulate sexual conversion under culture conditions.
source: Depletion of LysoPC or choline, a downstream metabolite in the same metabolic pathway, has now been used by several groups to stimulate sexual conversion under culture conditions (Brancucci et al., 2017; Filarsky et al., 2018; Portugaliza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Artemisinin and its derivatives are potent antimalarial drugs that rapidly kill asexual parasites.
source: Artemisinin and its derivatives (collectively referred to as ARTs) are potent antimalarial drugs that rapidly kill asexual parasites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about artemisinin drugs.

claim: After activation by cleavage of their endoperoxide bond by hemoglobin degradation products, ARTs produce reactive oxygen species and free radicals that result in widespread damage in parasite proteins and lipids.
source: After activation by cleavage of their endoperoxide bond by hemoglobin degradation products, ARTs produce reactive oxygen species and free radicals that result in widespread damage in parasite proteins and lipids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of artemisinin drugs.

claim: ARTs have a very short elimination half-life in the human circulation of approximately 1-3 hours.
source: However, because ARTs have a very short elimination half-life in the human circulation (~1–3 hr), their application as monotherapy was discontinued to avoid infection recrudescence and development of drug resistance.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge about artemisinin drugs.

claim: Application of ARTs as monotherapy was discontinued to avoid infection recrudescence and development of drug resistance.
source: However, because ARTs have a very short elimination half-life in the human circulation (~1–3 hr), their application as monotherapy was discontinued to avoid infection recrudescence and development of drug resistance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria treatment policy.

claim: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are the current frontline treatment for uncomplicated as well as severe malaria cases.
source: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), consisting of ART and a long-acting partner drug, are the current frontline treatment for uncomplicated as well as severe malaria cases (Blasco et al., 2017; de Vries and Dien, 1996; Haldar et al., 2018; Talman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and represents established treatment guidelines.

claim: Resistance to ARTs has emerged in South-East Asia in the form of delayed parasite clearance.
source: Resistance to ARTs has emerged in South-East Asia in the form of delayed parasite clearance (Dondorp et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: ART resistance is associated with mutations in the PfKelch13 protein.
source: ART resistance is associated with mutations in the PfKelch13 protein (Ariey et al., 2014) that prevent hemoglobin degradation in early ring-stage parasites.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: PfKelch13 mutations prevent hemoglobin degradation in early ring-stage parasites, which in turn prevents ART activation, resulting in resistance of early rings to the drug.
source: ART resistance is associated with mutations in the PfKelch13 protein (Ariey et al., 2014) that prevent hemoglobin degradation in early ring-stage parasites. This in turn prevents ART activation, resulting in resistance of early rings to the drug (Birnbaum et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: ART resistance is frequently accompanied by simultaneous resistance to partner drugs such as mefloquine, piperaquine, or amodiaquine.
source: Nowadays, ART resistance is frequently accompanied by simultaneous resistance to partner drugs such as mefloquine, piperaquine, or amodiaquine, resulting in high rates of treatment failure and limiting treatment options (Mairet-Khedim et al., 2020; Phyo et al., 2016; van der Pluijm et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Treatment with antimalarial drugs such as chloroquine or sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is usually associated with increased gametocytemia on the days following drug administration.
source: Treatment with antimalarial drugs such as chloroquine (CQ) or sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is usually associated with increased gametocytemia (density of gametocytes in the blood) on the days following drug administration, whereas treatment with ACTs results in reduced gametocytemia and transmission to mosquitoes (Ippolito et al., 2017; Okell et al., 2008; Price et al., 1996; Sawa et al., 2013; von Seidlein et al., 2001; WWARN Gametocyte Study Group, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Treatment with ACTs results in reduced gametocytemia and transmission to mosquitoes.
source: Treatment with antimalarial drugs such as chloroquine (CQ) or sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is usually associated with increased gametocytemia (density of gametocytes in the blood) on the days following drug administration, whereas treatment with ACTs results in reduced gametocytemia and transmission to mosquitoes (Ippolito et al., 2017; Okell et al., 2008; Price et al., 1996; Sawa et al., 2013; von Seidlein et al., 2001; WWARN Gametocyte Study Group, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Successfully treated patients can remain infectious for several days and contribute to transmission despite the efficacy of ACTs in reducing gametocytemia.
source: Despite the efficacy of ACTs in reducing gametocytemia, successfully treated patients can remain infectious for several days and contribute to transmission (Bousema et al., 2006; Bousema et al., 2010; Karl et al., 2015; Targett et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The higher capacity of ACTs to reduce gametocytemia compared to other drugs is attributable to faster killing of asexual parasites, more efficient killing of immature gametocytes, and partial clearance of mature gametocytes.
source: The higher capacity of ACTs to reduce gametocytemia compared to other drugs is attributable to several factors: (i) faster killing of asexual parasites, which prevents the formation of new gametocytes; (ii) more efficient killing of immature gametocytes; (iii) partial clearance of mature gametocytes, which are insensitive to most other clinically relevant drugs (Adjalley et al., 2011; Chotivanich et al., 2006; Plouffe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: There is no direct linear relationship between conversion rates and the prevalence and density of circulating gametocytes.
source: Although it has been proposed that the increase of gametocytemia observed after treatment with some drugs may reflect stimulation of sexual conversion, there is no direct linear relationship between conversion rates and the prevalence and density of circulating gametocytes (Carter et al., 2013; Koepfli and Yan, 2018; Reece and Schneider, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Gametocytes are sequestered away from the circulation until approximately 10 days after sexual conversion.
source: The dynamics of circulating gametocyte densities after treatment can be explained without invoking an adjustment of sexual conversion rates: first, gametocytes are sequestered away from the circulation until ~10 days after sexual conversion, implying that the peaks of gametocytemia observed after treatment with some drugs (within less than 10 days) may reflect the dynamics of asexual parasite growth before treatment, rather than post-treatment changes in sexual conversion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about gametocyte development and sequestration.

claim: The effects of drugs on sexual conversion rates in human infections cannot be disentangled from other drug-mediated actions such as the release of sequestered parasites or gametocyte clearance.
source: Second, the effects of the drugs on sexual conversion rates in human infections cannot be disentangled from other drug-mediated actions such as the release of sequestered parasites or gametocyte clearance (Babiker et al., 2008; Bousema and Drakeley, 2011; Butcher, 1997; Koepfli and Yan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: A small number of studies have used P. falciparum in vitro cultures to directly address the effect of drug treatment on sexual conversion, yielding inconsistent results.
source: To directly address the effect of drug treatment on sexual conversion, a small number of studies have used P. falciparum in vitro cultures, yielding inconsistent results.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Some studies reported increased sexual conversion upon exposure to specific doses of drugs such as CQ or ART.
source: While some studies reported increased sexual conversion upon exposure to specific doses of drugs such as CQ or ART (Buckling et al., 1999b; Peatey et al., 2009; Rajapandi, 2019), others did not observe this effect with ART (Brancucci et al., 2015), or reported reduced sexual conversion upon exposure to low doses of CQ or pyrimethamine (Reece et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Some studies did not observe increased sexual conversion with ART.
source: While some studies reported increased sexual conversion upon exposure to specific doses of drugs such as CQ or ART (Buckling et al., 1999b; Peatey et al., 2009; Rajapandi, 2019), others did not observe this effect with ART (Brancucci et al., 2015), or reported reduced sexual conversion upon exposure to low doses of CQ or pyrimethamine (Reece et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Some studies reported reduced sexual conversion upon exposure to low doses of CQ or pyrimethamine.
source: While some studies reported increased sexual conversion upon exposure to specific doses of drugs such as CQ or ART (Buckling et al., 1999b; Peatey et al., 2009; Rajapandi, 2019), others did not observe this effect with ART (Brancucci et al., 2015), or reported reduced sexual conversion upon exposure to low doses of CQ or pyrimethamine (Reece et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The divergent conclusions from previous studies suggest a complex scenario in which conditions such as the specific drug used, the parasite stage at the time of exposure, and drug concentration may determine the effect of treatment on sexual conversion.
source: Although the discrepancies may reflect methodological differences between these studies and limited accuracy in determining sexual conversion rates, the divergent conclusions also suggest a complex scenario in which conditions such as the specific drug used, the parasite stage at the time of exposure, and drug concentration may determine the effect of treatment on sexual conversion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inconsistent results in the literature.

claim: Understanding the impact of ARTs on the production of transmission forms is an urgent research priority given the widespread use of ACTs for malaria treatment and in mass drug administration campaigns.
source: Given the widespread use of ACTs for malaria treatment and in mass drug administration campaigns aimed at malaria elimination, understanding the impact of ARTs on sexual conversion is an urgent research priority.
evidence: This is a statement about research priorities based on the practical importance of ACTs.

claim: The authors developed a robust assay based on gametocyte-reporter parasite lines to accurately measure the impact of drugs on sexual conversion rates, independently from their gametocytocidal activity.
source: Here we developed a robust assay based on recently described gametocyte-reporter parasite lines (Portugaliza et al., 2019) to accurately measure the impact of drugs on sexual conversion rates, independently from their gametocytocidal activity.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology developed in this study.

claim: Exposure to subcurative doses of dihydroartemisinin (DHA) at the trophozoite stage resulted in a ~fourfold increase in sexual conversion.
source: We found that exposure to subcurative doses of the frontline antimalarial drug dihydroartemisinin (DHA) at the trophozoite stage resulted in a ~ fourfold increase in sexual conversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: No increase in sexual conversion was observed when ring stages were exposed to DHA.
source: In contrast, no increase was observed when ring stages were exposed or in cultures in which sexual conversion was stimulated by choline depletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: No increase in sexual conversion was observed in cultures in which sexual conversion was stimulated by choline depletion.
source: In contrast, no increase was observed when ring stages were exposed or in cultures in which sexual conversion was stimulated by choline depletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The results reveal a complex relationship between antimalarial drugs and sexual conversion, with potential public health implications.
source: Our results reveal a complex relationship between antimalarial drugs and sexual conversion, with potential public health implications.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In cultures supplemented with choline, the sexual conversion rate increased from <10% in control cultures to ~40% in cultures exposed to a 5 or 10 nM DHA pulse at the trophozoite stage.
source: In cultures supplemented with choline, the sexual conversion rate increased from <10% in control cultures to ~40% in cultures exposed to a 5 or 10 nM DHA pulse at the trophozoite stage (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Total gametocytemia was clearly higher in DHA-exposed cultures than in control cultures.
source: Importantly, total gametocytemia (determined at the next multiplication cycle after drug exposure, i.e., early gametocytes) was also clearly higher in DHA-exposed cultures than in control cultures (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The increase in the sexual conversion rate is not only attributable to the lower number of asexual parasites after drug treatment, but also to a net increase in the number of gametocytes produced.
source: This result indicates that the increase in the sexual conversion rate is not only attributable to the lower number of asexual parasites after drug treatment, but also to a net increase in the number of gametocytes produced.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In cultures in which sexual conversion was already stimulated by choline depletion, DHA treatment did not result in a further increase in the sexual conversion rate or in the absolute number of gametocytes.
source: By contrast, in cultures in which sexual conversion was already stimulated by choline depletion, DHA treatment did not result in a further increase in the sexual conversion rate or in the absolute number of gametocytes (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: A 2 nM DHA pulse did not have a measurable effect on parasite growth.
source: A 2 nM DHA pulse did not have a measurable effect on parasite growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), but in choline-supplemented cultures it consistently resulted in a > twofold increase in the sexual conversion rate and the total number of gametocytes (although not statistically significant; Figure 1—figure supplement 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: In choline-supplemented cultures, a 2 nM DHA pulse consistently resulted in a >twofold increase in the sexual conversion rate and the total number of gametocytes (although not statistically significant).
source: A 2 nM DHA pulse did not have a measurable effect on parasite growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), but in choline-supplemented cultures it consistently resulted in a > twofold increase in the sexual conversion rate and the total number of gametocytes (although not statistically significant; Figure 1—figure supplement 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-D.

claim: Drug doses <2 nM did not have a detectable effect on sexual conversion.
source: Drug doses < 2 nM did not have a detectable effect on sexual conversion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: In choline-supplemented cultures, both sexual conversion rates and total gametocytemia were clearly enhanced upon exposure to DHA concentrations up to 15 nM.
source: In choline-supplemented cultures, both sexual conversion rates and total gametocytemia were clearly enhanced upon exposure to DHA concentrations up to 15 nM, but the increase was lower upon exposure to higher concentrations.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The increase in sexual conversion was lower upon exposure to DHA concentrations higher than 15 nM.
source: In choline-supplemented cultures, both sexual conversion rates and total gametocytemia were clearly enhanced upon exposure to DHA concentrations up to 15 nM, but the increase was lower upon exposure to higher concentrations.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: In choline-depleted cultures, increasing DHA doses resulted in a progressive reduction of sexual conversion.
source: In choline-depleted cultures, increasing DHA doses resulted in a progressive reduction of sexual conversion (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C-D.

claim: Gametocytes of the NF54-gexp02-Tom line produced in cultures treated with 5 nM DHA at the trophozoite stage matured through stages I to V without any apparent morphological alteration.
source: Gametocytes of the NF54-gexp02-Tom line produced in cultures treated with 5 nM DHA at the trophozoite stage (in the presence of choline) matured through stages I to V without any apparent morphological alteration.
evidence: This is based on microscopic observations of gametocyte morphology.

claim: Mature, stage V gametocytes from DHA-treated cultures were able to exflagellate after activation and to infect mosquitoes productively.
source: Furthermore, mature, stage V gametocytes were able to exflagellate after activation and to infect mosquitoes productively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The gametocytemia 10-13 days later (mature gametocytes) and the number of exflagellation centers were higher in DHA-treated cultures compared to control cultures.
source: As expected from the increase in the number of early gametocytes in DHA-treated cultures, the gametocytemia 10–13 d later (mature gametocytes) and the number of exflagellation centers were also higher in DHA-treated cultures compared to control cultures (no DHA).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: The number of oocysts and sporozoites per mosquito was higher in mosquitoes fed with DHA-treated cultures than in mosquitoes fed with control cultures.
source: Likewise, when using these cultures to infect mosquitoes, the number of oocysts and sporozoites per mosquito was higher in mosquitoes fed with DHA-treated cultures than in mosquitoes fed with control cultures.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements from mosquito infections.

claim: The magnitude of the increase in oocysts and sporozoites was similar to that observed in mosquitoes fed with cultures in which sexual conversion was stimulated by choline depletion.
source: The magnitude of the increase was similar to that observed in mosquitoes fed with cultures in which sexual conversion was stimulated by choline depletion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A DHA pulse (5 or 10 nM) at the early ring stage that reduced growth by <25% did not enhance sexual conversion.
source: A DHA pulse (5 or 10 nM) at the early ring stage that reduced growth by <25% (Figure 3A–B) did not enhance sexual conversion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: DHA pulse at the early ring stage resulted in a reduction of sexual conversion and gametocytemia, both in choline-supplemented and choline-depleted cultures.
source: Instead, it resulted in a reduction of sexual conversion and gametocytemia, both in choline-supplemented and choline-depleted NF54-gexp02-Tom cultures (Figure 3C–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference between sexual conversion determined at 24 and 48 hpi, excluding the possibility that the lower conversion rates observed in cultures exposed to DHA at the ring stage are attributable to a DHA-induced delay in sexual conversion or gametocyte development.
source: In these experiments, we determined sexual conversion by measuring expression of the gametocyte reporter at 24 and 48 hr post invasion (hpi), and observed no difference between sexual conversion determined at the two different time points. This result excludes the possibility that the lower conversion rates observed in cultures exposed to DHA at the ring stage are attributable to a DHA-induced delay in sexual conversion or gametocyte development (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: DHA exposure at the early ring stage did not stimulate immediate sexual conversion via the same cycle conversion (SCC) pathway.
source: To explore the possibility that DHA exposure at the early ring stage may stimulate immediate sexual conversion via the same cycle conversion (SCC) pathway (Bancells et al., 2019), rather than by the canonical next cycle conversion (NCC) pathway, we assessed the effect of DHA exposure at the ring stage on the level of gametocytes produced within the same cycle of exposure (Figure 4A). We observed no apparent differences in sexual conversion rates via the SCC route between DHA-exposed cultures and their controls (Figure 4B–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Choline depletion did not increase sexual conversion via the SCC route.
source: In these experiments, choline depletion did not increase sexual conversion via the SCC route (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Choline depletion at the ring stage does not induce sexual conversion, in contrast to depletion at the trophozoite stage.
source: We found that choline depletion at the ring stage does not induce sexual conversion, in contrast to depletion at the trophozoite stage (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Parasites at the ring stage are largely insensitive to environmental stimulation of sexual conversion.
source: Altogether, these results show that in parasites at the ring stage neither a DHA pulse nor choline depletion induces sexual conversion, suggesting that this developmental stage is largely insensitive to environmental stimulation of sexual conversion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Exposure to 80 nM CQ at the trophozoite stage, a dose that induces ~40% lethality, resulted in enhanced sexual conversion rates in choline-supplemented cultures.
source: Exposure to 80 nM CQ at the trophozoite stage, a dose that induces ~40% lethality (Figure 6B), resulted in enhanced sexual conversion rates in choline-supplemented cultures (Figure 6C–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The level of induction by CQ was only ~twofold, much lower than induction by DHA.
source: However, the level of induction was only ~ twofold, much lower than induction by DHA, and there was no consistent induction at higher or lower drug doses.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental results.

claim: CQ exposure at the trophozoite stage did not increase sexual conversion in choline-depleted cultures.
source: Similar to DHA, CQ exposure at the trophozoite stage did not increase sexual conversion in choline-depleted cultures (Figure 6C–D), and exposure to CQ at the ring stage did not enhance sexual conversion by either the NCC or the SCC (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–3) routes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Exposure to CQ at the ring stage did not enhance sexual conversion by either the NCC or the SCC routes.
source: Similar to DHA, CQ exposure at the trophozoite stage did not increase sexual conversion in choline-depleted cultures (Figure 6C–D), and exposure to CQ at the ring stage did not enhance sexual conversion by either the NCC or the SCC (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–3) routes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2-3.

claim: Exposure of choline-supplemented cultures at the trophozoite stage to heat shock at 41.5°C, which reduced survival by ~40%, resulted in a ~fourfold increase in sexual conversion and gametocytemia.
source: Exposure of choline-supplemented cultures at the trophozoite stage to heat shock, which reduced survival by ~40%, resulted in a ~ fourfold increase in sexual conversion and gametocytemia (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A subcurative DHA pulse at the trophozoite stage resulted in upregulation of both pfap2-g and gexp02 relative to the serine-tRNA ligase reference gene in choline-supplemented cultures, but not in choline-depleted cultures.
source: A subcurative DHA pulse at the trophozoite stage resulted in upregulation of both pfap2-g and gexp02 relative to the serine-tRNA ligase (PF3D7_0717700) reference gene in choline-supplemented cultures, but not in choline-depleted cultures (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Exposure to DHA at the ring stage resulted in reduced expression of both pfap2-g and gexp02.
source: By contrast, exposure to DHA at the ring stage resulted in reduced expression of both genes (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: Analysis of transcripts only 2 hr after DHA exposure at the ring stage did not reveal induction of pfap2-g or gexp02.
source: Analysis of transcripts only 2 hr after DHA exposure at the ring stage did not reveal induction of pfap2-g or gexp02 (Figure 8G–I), ruling out activation of the genes at a time consistent with conversion via the SCC route.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8G-I.

claim: The findings of transcriptional analyses clearly mirror the effect of the drug on sexual conversion rates, indicating that induction of sexual conversion by DHA is associated with pfap2-g activation.
source: Overall, the findings of these transcriptional analyses clearly mirror the effect of the drug on sexual conversion rates, indicating that induction of sexual conversion by DHA is associated with pfap2-g activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between transcriptional and phenotypic data.

claim: The overall impact of a drug on the transmission potential of an infection depends on its effect on the sexual conversion rate and on several other factors.
source: The overall impact of a drug on the transmission potential of an infection depends on its effect on the sexual conversion rate, and on several other factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of drug effects on transmission.

claim: The stimulation of sexual commitment at the trophozoite stage may not result in an overall increase in transmission due to rapid clearance of asexual parasites and activity of the drug against developing and mature gametocytes.
source: In the case of ARTs, the stimulation of sexual commitment at the trophozoite stage may not result in an overall increase in transmission due to rapid clearance of asexual parasites, which prevents new rounds of gametocyte production, and to the activity of the drug against developing and mature gametocytes.
evidence: This is an inference about the net effect of ARTs on transmission based on their multiple mechanisms of action.

claim: Several studies have observed that treatment with drug combinations containing ARTs reduce gametocyte density and the duration of gametocyte carriage.
source: Indeed, several studies have observed that treatment with drug combinations containing ARTs reduce gametocyte density and the duration of gametocyte carriage (Bousema et al., 2006; Bousema et al., 2010; Ippolito et al., 2017; Karl et al., 2015; Okell et al., 2008; Price et al., 1996; Sawa et al., 2013; Targett et al., 2001; von Seidlein et al., 2001; WWARN Gametocyte Study Group, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Patients in which many of the parasites are at the trophozoite stage at the time of ART administration may experience a peak of circulating gametocytes ~10 days after treatment if the drug does not kill all parasites.
source: Notwithstanding the net reduction of transmission potential commonly observed after ART treatment, it is possible that patients in which many of the parasites are at the trophozoite stage at the time of ART administration may experience a peak of circulating gametocytes ~ 10 days after treatment (the time required for gametocyte maturation), if the drug does not kill all parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the study findings and knowledge of gametocyte maturation timing.

claim: The largest stimulation of sexual conversion was observed at subcurative doses of the drug.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that the largest stimulation of sexual conversion was observed at subcurative doses of the drug.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: Low drug concentrations may occur during treatment with substandard or underdosed drugs, through poor compliance with the prescribed regimen, as a consequence of drug malabsorption, or as the drug is eliminated following its natural pharmacokinetics profile.
source: Such low drug concentrations may occur during treatment with substandard or underdosed drugs, through poor compliance with the prescribed regimen, as a consequence of drug malabsorption, or as the drug is eliminated following its natural pharmacokinetics profile.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of factors affecting drug concentrations in clinical settings.

claim: Treatment associated with low ARTs concentration may enable survival of some parasites, and at the same time enhance the probability of sexual conversion.
source: Treatment associated with low ARTs concentration may enable survival of some parasites, and at the same time enhance the probability of sexual conversion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study findings.

claim: The findings have potential public health implications for the use of ARTs in treatment and elimination strategies.
source: Thus, our findings have potential public health implications for the use of ARTs in treatment and elimination strategies.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the study findings.

claim: The benefits of ARTs for malaria treatment clearly outweigh the potential risks.
source: While the benefits of ARTs for malaria treatment clearly outweigh the potential risks, the possibility that ARTs increase the transmission potential of some patients should be taken into account when considering their massive use in preventive treatment or elimination campaigns.
evidence: This is a statement balancing the study findings with established knowledge about ART efficacy.

claim: The possibility that ARTs increase the transmission potential of some patients should be taken into account when considering their massive use in preventive treatment or elimination campaigns.
source: While the benefits of ARTs for malaria treatment clearly outweigh the potential risks, the possibility that ARTs increase the transmission potential of some patients should be taken into account when considering their massive use in preventive treatment or elimination campaigns.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Experiments with P. falciparum exposed to low doses of DHA at the ring stage were consistent with predictions of evolutionary theory for life histories, showing moderately reduced sexual conversion rates.
source: Our experiments with in vitro cultured P. falciparum exposed to low doses of DHA at the ring stage were also consistent with these prediction, as this resulted in moderately reduced sexual conversion rates.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: Experiments in which a pulse of DHA or CQ at a low dose was administered at the trophozoite stage showed the opposite trend to evolutionary theory predictions, such that the subcurative treatment stimulated sexual conversion.
source: In contrast, experiments in which a pulse of DHA or CQ at a low dose was administered at the trophozoite stage showed the opposite trend, such that the subcurative treatment stimulated sexual conversion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: The results with P. falciparum exposed to low doses of DHA or CQ at the trophozoite stage are in line with some previous studies using P. falciparum or a murine malaria model.
source: This latter result is in line with some previous studies using P. falciparum (Buckling et al., 1999b; Peatey et al., 2009) or a murine malaria model (Buckling et al., 1999a; Buckling et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In the absence of stress, sexual conversion in P. falciparum is already restrained, with estimated conversion rates of ~1% in human infections.
source: A possible explanation for the discrepancy with the predictions of evolutionary theory (when exposure occurs at the trophozoite stage) is that in the absence of stress, sexual conversion in P. falciparum is already restrained, with estimated conversion rates of ~1% in human infections (Cao et al., 2019; Eichner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: A further reduction of the investment in transmission upon exposure to low drug doses would not have a substantial impact on within-host survival, implying that this response would not provide a selective advantage.
source: Thus, a further reduction of the investment in transmission upon exposure to low drug doses would not have a substantial impact on within-host survival, implying that this response would not provide a selective advantage, whereas the opposite response can enhance the chances of transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary reasoning.

claim: The absence of LysoPC and choline, or heat shock, all of which reduce the multiplication rate of P. falciparum cultures, also stimulate sexual conversion.
source: Of note, the absence of LysoPC and choline (Brancucci et al., 2017), or heat shock, all of which reduce the multiplication rate of P. falciparum cultures and therefore can also be considered as sublethal stress signals, also stimulate sexual conversion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and experimental data from this study.

claim: The results of experiments with P. falciparum cultures exposed to low level of stress at the trophozoite stage do not support the predictions of evolutionary theory.
source: Together, the results of experiments with P. falciparum cultures exposed to low level of stress at the trophozoite stage do not support the predictions of evolutionary theory, whereas for murine malaria parasites different studies reported conflicting results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison with theory.

claim: Different Plasmodium species may use different strategies to adjust sexual conversion rates upon stress.
source: In this regard, it is possible that different Plasmodium species use different strategies to adjust sexual conversion rates upon stress: although the role of AP2-G as the master regulator of sexual conversion appears to be widely conserved in all malaria parasite species, upstream events involved in the regulation of sexual conversion are remarkably different between human and murine parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known differences between species.

claim: The role of AP2-G as the master regulator of sexual conversion appears to be widely conserved in all malaria parasite species.
source: In this regard, it is possible that different Plasmodium species use different strategies to adjust sexual conversion rates upon stress: although the role of AP2-G as the master regulator of sexual conversion appears to be widely conserved in all malaria parasite species, upstream events involved in the regulation of sexual conversion are remarkably different between human and murine parasites.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about AP2-G function across species.

claim: Upstream events involved in the regulation of sexual conversion are remarkably different between human and murine parasites.
source: In this regard, it is possible that different Plasmodium species use different strategies to adjust sexual conversion rates upon stress: although the role of AP2-G as the master regulator of sexual conversion appears to be widely conserved in all malaria parasite species, upstream events involved in the regulation of sexual conversion are remarkably different between human and murine parasites.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about differences in sexual conversion regulation.

claim: Murine malaria parasites show higher conversion rates, do not alter sexual conversion in response to LysoPC restriction, and their genomes lack a gdv1 ortholog.
source: The latter show higher conversion rates, do not alter sexual conversion in response to LysoPC restriction, and their genomes lack a gdv1 ortholog (Ngotho et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Sexual conversion can be stimulated by exposure to DHA at the trophozoite stage, but not at the early ring stage.
source: Our experiments establish that sexual conversion can be stimulated by exposure to DHA at the trophozoite stage, but not at the early ring stage.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Stimulation of sexual conversion by depletion of choline or by exposure to CQ shows a similar stage dependency to DHA.
source: Of note, stimulation of sexual conversion by depletion of choline (as a proxy for LysoPC depletion) or by exposure to CQ shows a similar stage dependency, suggesting that the ring stage is largely insensitive to stimulation of sexual conversion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: At the ring stage, some types of stress, such as exposure to DHA, may induce latency of a rather small fraction of the parasites as a means of population survival.
source: At the ring stage, some types of stress, such as exposure to DHA, may induce latency of a rather small fraction of the parasites as a means of population survival (Barrett et al., 2019; Talman et al., 2019), rather than enhancing sexual conversion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and represents a speculative interpretation.

claim: In cultures in which sexual conversion is stimulated by choline depletion, it cannot be further stimulated by drugs, such that there are no additive or synergistic effects between drugs and choline depletion.
source: Furthermore, we found that in cultures in which sexual conversion is stimulated by choline depletion, it cannot be further stimulated by drugs, such that there are no additive or synergistic effects between drugs and choline depletion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The different stimuli converge into the same mechanism of pfap2-g activation, which likely involves cellular components that are absent during the ring stage.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the different stimuli converge into the same mechanism of pfap2-g activation, which likely involves cellular components that are absent during the ring stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Stimulation by DHA may depend on GDV1.
source: Because stimulation of sexual conversion by choline depletion has been shown to involve GDV1 (Filarsky et al., 2018), which is only expressed in the second half of the intraerythrocytic development cycle and is absent from ring stage parasites, we hypothesize that stimulation by DHA may also depend on GDV1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known mechanisms and the study findings.

claim: Treatment with DHA may result in choline depletion because DHA induces damage on membrane lipids, which may increase the use of LysoPC or choline, resulting in a reduction of their levels.
source: A possible explanation for the similar effects of DHA and choline depletion on sexual conversion is that treatment with DHA may result in choline depletion: DHA induces damage on membrane lipids (Hartwig et al., 2009), which may increase the use of LysoPC or choline, resulting in a reduction of their levels.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation about DHA's effects on lipids.

claim: Heat shock, a completely different type of stress that is not known or predicted to affect LysoPC or choline levels, also enhanced sexual conversion.
source: However, heat shock, a completely different type of stress that is not known or predicted to affect LysoPC or choline levels, also enhanced sexual conversion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: Stimulation of sexual conversion can occur without the involvement of choline metabolism.
source: This result suggests that stimulation of sexual conversion can occur without the involvement of choline metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the heat shock experiment results.

claim: Parasites may be able to sense a state of mild to moderate 'stress' or growth restriction.
source: As an alternative model, parasites may be able to sense a state of mild to moderate 'stress' or growth restriction (Schneider et al., 2018): the drug doses that result in increased sexual conversion, as well as LysoPC or choline restriction (Brancucci et al., 2017; Portugaliza et al., 2019) and heat shock, were all associated with a < 50% reduction of growth rates.
evidence: This is a speculative model supported by citations and experimental observations.

claim: The observation that a 2 nM pulse of DHA, which does not have any measurable effect on parasite survival, appears to stimulate sexual conversion may indicate that sexual conversion is triggered by the response associated with moderate stress, rather than by growth restriction per se.
source: The observation that a 2 nM pulse of DHA, which does not have any measurable effect on parasite survival, appears to stimulate sexual conversion may indicate that sexual conversion is triggered by the response associated with moderate stress, rather than by growth restriction per se.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Activation of the cellular stress response has been proposed to be associated with enhanced gametocyte production.
source: In this regard, activation of the cellular stress response has been proposed to be associated with enhanced gametocyte production (Chaubey et al., 2014), and DHA triggers such a stress response (Bridgford et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: DHA triggers a cellular stress response.
source: In this regard, activation of the cellular stress response has been proposed to be associated with enhanced gametocyte production (Chaubey et al., 2014), and DHA triggers such a stress response (Bridgford et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The study provides a detailed characterization of the changes in P. falciparum sexual conversion rates that occur in response to a pulse of DHA.
source: Altogether, here we provide a detailed characterization of the changes in P. falciparum sexual conversion rates that occur in response to a pulse of DHA.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution.

claim: The study demonstrates remarkable plasticity in sexual conversion rates.
source: We demonstrate remarkable plasticity in sexual conversion rates, and a complex response that depends on the stage of the parasites at the time when they are exposed to the drug, the drug dose, and the metabolic state (presence or absence of choline).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The response to DHA depends on the stage of the parasites at the time of exposure, the drug dose, and the metabolic state.
source: We demonstrate remarkable plasticity in sexual conversion rates, and a complex response that depends on the stage of the parasites at the time when they are exposed to the drug, the drug dose, and the metabolic state (presence or absence of choline).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: This complex scenario may explain the discrepant results obtained by previous studies.
source: This complex scenario may explain the discrepant results obtained by previous studies.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the study findings for understanding previous literature.

claim: The assay developed to test the impact of DHA on sexual conversion rates can be used to test the impact of any other drug or condition.
source: The assay that we have developed to test the impact of DHA on sexual conversion rates can be used to test the impact of any other drug or condition, as shown here for CQ and heat shock.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader applicability of the methodology.

claim: The success of malaria elimination efforts largely depends on the ability to reduce or interrupt transmission.
source: Of note, the success of malaria elimination efforts largely depends on the ability to reduce or interrupt transmission.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria elimination strategies.

claim: The overall impact of treatment with ACTs is a reduction of the transmission potential, at least when compared with other drugs.
source: Although our results are not of immediate public health concern because the overall impact of treatment with ACTs is a reduction of the transmission potential, at least when compared with other drugs, the capacity of ARTs to induce sexual conversion must be taken into account.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from clinical studies.

claim: Under certain conditions, treatment may result in an increase in transmission that could jeopardize efforts to eliminate malaria.
source: Otherwise, under certain conditions, treatment may result in an increase in transmission that could jeopardize efforts to eliminate malaria.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings.
